title: the lac house
hook: a feast, a family of strangers asleep, and a fire lit from the inside
carry: a woman and five sons, unnamed

segments.voice: Yesterday, the lac house: the brothers staying calm on the surface while a passage was dug under the floor. Did you quietly prepare a way out of something? Day seven hundred thirty-seven.

The house at Varanavata was made to look like a gift and to burn like a torch, with lac and resin and ghee worked into its walls, the text says. Under its floor there's a secret of a different kind: a tunnel, dug by a miner Vidura sent, its mouth hidden inside the house. Kunti and her sons have been living on top of a fire that hasn't been lit yet. Purochana, the man who built it, is living there too, waiting for his moment. Tonight, someone else strikes first.
screen: `A HOUSE MADE TO BURN.` → `A TUNNEL UNDER THE FLOOR.` → `TONIGHT.`

segments.voice: Kunti gives a feast. Brahmins come and eat, and women come, and when it's over, the guests go home. But a Nishada woman, a woman of the forest people, has come looking for food with her five sons. They eat and drink, and they fall asleep in the house, so heavily, the text says, they're like the dead. Then, in the dark, Bhima gets up. He sets fire first to the place where Purochana is sleeping. Then to the door. Then all around the house. And the family goes down into the tunnel, and out. In the morning the townspeople stand at the ashes, grieving. They find Purochana, burned in his own trap. And they find a woman and five young men, and they say: Kunti and her sons are dead. That's the escape. Now stay with one detail. The plan works because strangers were in the house. The text tells it quickly, and doesn't stop for them. Some readers take it plainly: fate put those bodies there, and the story needed the world to believe. Some say the poem is letting us see the cost of the cousins' quarrel, beginning with people who had no part in it. Some notice that the woman and her sons are never named, and that the silence is itself worth hearing. Here the poem doesn't pause to rule on the act. It shows it, and leaves room. The lac house was built to kill the Pandavas. It ends up killing the man who built it, and six people nobody planned for.
screen: `A FEAST, AND GUESTS WHO STAY.` · `BHIMA LIGHTS THE FIRE.` · `SIX BODIES IN THE ASHES.` · then, large: `THE ONES WITH NO NAMES.`

segments.voice: There's a cost in this story, so take it slowly. Let the breath settle. Bring to mind someone caught up in something that wasn't theirs: a stranger in the news, a person in the background of your own day, someone whose name you never learned. You don't need to fix anything. Just hold them in attention for a while, the way the story doesn't stop to. If you pray, you can hold them there. The bell holds the time.
Nishada, a woman of the forest people who slept in the house that night, with her five sons, and was never named.
Your line: a woman and five sons, unnamed. Today, learn the name of one person you usually pass without one. Day seven hundred thirty-seven.

howItsDone: Some Hindus read the Mahabharata straight through over months, a section at a time, as this serial does; others meet episodes like the lac house through storytelling, theater and television.

match.prompt: the night of the fire — tap the pairs.
pairs: falls asleep there with her sons

myth: Bhima did, starting where Purochana slept.
the family escaped through a tunnel
dug in secret under the house, its mouth hidden inside.
the townspeople knew the Pandavas had survived
they found the bodies and believed Kunti and her sons were dead.

fork.setup: you're Bhima. the house is quiet, the guests are asleep, and Purochana is waiting for his chance. what do you do?
options: wait for Purochana to make the first move.
light the fire first, and take the tunnel.
wake the guests and send them home.
fork.reveal: he lit the fire himself, starting where Purochana slept. the guests stayed asleep, and the town later took their bodies for the Pandavas'.

original.note: Sanskrit niṣāda: a name for forest-dwelling peoples; the woman who sleeps in the house is a Nishada.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Pandavas escaped, and that's the whole story.
what it means: they got away because a woman and her five sons slept in the house, and burned in their place.
what a scholar hears: the text never names them, and the town's mistake about their bodies is what lets the Pandavas vanish.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Jatugriha Parva (the feast, the Nishada woman and her sons, Bhima sets the fire, the escape through the tunnel, the townspeople at the ashes)

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm in Ganguli: the materials of the house (lac, resin, ghee), the miner sent by Vidura, the feast for brahmanas, the Nishada woman with five sons sleeping 'like the dead', and the order of the fire (Purochana's place, the door, then all around).
Days 734–736 (another writer) cover the plot, Vidura's riddle and the tunnel; this day takes the night of the fire.
'Six people' is derived from the text's woman and five sons; confirm.
The three 'some readers' takes are unattributed interpretations, given without ranking; a Keeper may wish to adjust the framing of the Nishada woman's death.

Editor pass: 'Brahmanas' made 'Brahmins' for consistency; cut 'the part that's hard to read past' (told the listener what they feel) and the general claim that the Mahabharata 'often works like this'.
